title: Article 14 — Equality before law (Fundamental Rights subject)

content.overview: Article 14 says the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It binds the State and protects any person, not only citizens. Equal protection permits a rational classification that has an intelligible differentia and a rational nexus with the object of the law. Arbitrariness is the usual teaching contrast with permissible classification. Those tests are case-law and are not given a verified ratio in this file.
content.study: Ask who is denied what, by which State instrument, and how the compared class is drawn. Article 14 is not Article 15. Non-citizens can plead Article 14.

sections.heading: Reasonable classification
sections.body: Intelligible differentia; rational relation to object.

sections.heading: Golden triangle
sections.body: Articles 14, 19 and 21 read together when liberty or freedom is challenged (Maneka Gandhi).

learningObjectives: State the two clauses of Article 14.
Identify the person, the State and the comparison.
Keep classification doctrine on the case-law gate.
enhancement.definition: Article 14 forbids the State to deny equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws to any person in India.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The article is a State duty owed to persons. It does not itself list forbidden grounds. Those are Article 15.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Constitution of India, Article 14. Articles 15 and 16 are specific equality guarantees.
essentialIngredients: Article 15 or 16 used if a listed ground or public employment is the real claim
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Equality before the law is the rule that the State does not place a person above the law. Equal protection is the rule that like cases are treated alike. The article uses 'any person', so citizenship is not required. A classification defence, if raised, must be examined from authority; this note records only that teaching distinguishes reasonable classification from arbitrariness and does not adopt a case. Special provisions under Articles 15(3), 15(4), 15(5), 15(6) and 16(4) are not automatically Article 14 violations; they are authorised by those articles.
examples: A licence rule singles out one trader with no stated differentia. Article 14 is the plea.
A non-citizen is excluded from a general legal protection. Article 14 can apply; Article 15 may not, because Article 15 uses citizens.
A women-only hostel is challenged under Article 14. Article 15(3) is the neighbouring provision.
enhancement.problemApplication: Find the State act, the person, and the comparator. If the ground is religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, open Article 15 as well.
distinctions: Article 14 any person vs Article 15 citizens
Equality before law vs equal protection
Classification defence vs an Article 15 special provision
